# PoC B — synchronous HTTP ingress backed by a durable Temporal Workflow

Proves: an ordinary synchronous HTTP request/response can be backed
end-to-end by a real `executeFlow` Temporal Workflow, with the HTTP
response only written after `handle.result()` resolves - and that this
survives an Activity worker restart mid-flight, an ingress-process death,
and a client disconnect, all without corrupting the Workflow's own
durable execution.

Complements PoC A (`poc/http-ingress/`, fire-and-forget `202` + async
completion). This PoC (`poc/http-ingress-b/`) is the synchronous
counterpart: the HTTP client blocks until the flow completes and gets the
flow's own response descriptor as the real HTTP response.

## Files

- `flow.json` — PoC flow: `n1` (function, builds request context) ->
  `n5` (delay, configurable) -> `n3` (function, builds the response
  descriptor `{statusCode, headers, payload}`) -> `n4` (function, no-op
  sink, wires `n3`'s send so it gets captured - see "Shortcut" below).
- `sync-server.js` — Node built-in `http` server exposing `POST /poc/sync`:
  serializes the request into an envelope, starts `executeFlow`, `await`s
  `handle.result()`, writes the real HTTP response from the descriptor.
- `run-worker.js` — thin wrapper around `createCombinedWorker` (same
  function `bin/node-red-temporal worker --role combined` uses) that also
  passes `captureOptions.timeoutMs`, which the CLI does not expose as a
  flag - needed because this PoC's `delay` node intentionally runs past
  `capture.js`'s 5s default.
- `README.md` — this file.

No new dependency was added. `express` already exists in the monorepo's
node_modules (a transitive Node-RED dependency, used by PoC A), but this
PoC deliberately avoids relying on that hoisting detail and uses Node's
built-in `http` module instead.

## The shortcut: getting a response payload out of `handle.result()`

`executeFlow`'s Workflow code only ever returned `{flowVersion, lastNode}`
- no msg content. Node-RED's `preRoute` hook (which Capture uses to record
`sends`) only fires for WIRED destinations, so a truly wireless terminal
node's output msg is never captured anywhere Activity results can see.

**Chosen: Option 1** (recommended in the task), with one addition:

1. `lib/workflows.js`'s `runFlow` now also tracks `lastMsg` - the msg
   actually emitted by whichever node executes last - and returns it
   alongside `{flowVersion, lastNode}`. Every change is loudly marked
   `// POC ONLY — poc/http-ingress-b — do not merge as production API`
   (full diff below).
2. Because `lastMsg` is derived from `send.msg` (the msg a node handed to
   `node.send()`, captured via the existing `preRoute` hook), the flow's
   true terminal node (`n3`, which builds the response descriptor) is
   wired to a trivial no-op sink node (`n4`) purely so its send gets
   captured by Capture at all. `n4` does nothing with the msg; it exists
   only to give `n3`'s output a wire to be captured on. `lastMsg` ends up
   being exactly `n3`'s output payload - the response descriptor.
3. `sync-server.js` reads `result.lastMsg.payload` (`{statusCode, headers,
   payload}`) and writes it as the real HTTP response.

This keeps the diff to a few lines and does not require any new
architecture (no side-channel file/map, no new Activity type).

### Full diff outside `poc/http-ingress-b/`

Only `lib/workflows.js` was touched (all changes loudly marked POC ONLY):

```diff
@@ -154,6 +154,12 @@ async function runFlow({ executeNode, createExecuteNode, graph, nodeMeta, flowVe

+    // POC ONLY — poc/http-ingress-b — do not merge as production API.
+    // Tracks the msg delivered to whichever node executes last (i.e. the
+    // final in-flight payload), so a synchronous HTTP bridge can read a
+    // response descriptor back out of `handle.result()` without a
+    // side-channel. See poc/http-ingress-b/README.md for rationale.
+    let lastMsg;

     while (wave.length) {

@@ -212,8 +218,17 @@ async function runFlow({ executeNode, createExecuteNode, graph, nodeMeta, flowVe
                 });
             }

+            // POC ONLY — poc/http-ingress-b — do not merge as production API.
+            // Falls back to this node's OWN input msg when it has no sends
+            // (a true wireless terminal node) - overwritten below by the
+            // more accurate "msg actually sent onward" whenever sends exist.
+            lastMsg = current.msg;
             const sends = result.sends || [];

@@ -239,7 +254,8 @@ async function runFlow({ executeNode, createExecuteNode, graph, nodeMeta, flowVe
         wave = nextWave;
     }

-    return { flowVersion, lastNode };
+    // POC ONLY — poc/http-ingress-b — do not merge as production API.
+    return { flowVersion, lastNode, lastMsg };
 }

@@ -247,8 +263,14 @@ async function runFlow({ executeNode, createExecuteNode, graph, nodeMeta, flowVe
 // capture.js) so a NODE_TIMEOUT from Capture always surfaces first, instead

+// POC ONLY — poc/http-ingress-b — do not merge as production API. Bumped

+// attempt + one successful retry) - kept comfortably above the PoC's own
+// Capture `timeoutMs` (see run-worker.js) so NODE_TIMEOUT still surfaces
+// first per the ordering comment above.
 const BASE_ACTIVITY_OPTIONS = {
-    startToCloseTimeout: "30s",
+    startToCloseTimeout: "40s",
     // Retry policy for transient infra failures (thrown Activity errors,
     // e.g. worker crash mid-call). Node-level business errors never throw

```

The `startToCloseTimeout` bump (30s -> 40s) is a real, if small, behavior
change to shared production code, not just additive - flagged clearly here
and in-line. It only matters for flows with `delay`/long-running nodes
close to the 30s boundary; every existing test still passes 40s as easily
as 30s for its own short-lived Activities (verified below).

## Environment / ports used (isolated from PoC A and the coordinator's own Temporal)

| Component | Value |
|---|---|
| Temporal dev server | `temporal server start-dev --port 7249 --ui-port 8249 --db-filename /tmp/poc-http-ingress-b-temporal.db` |
| `TEMPORAL_ADDRESS` | `127.0.0.1:7249` |
| `TEMPORAL_WORKFLOW_TASK_QUEUE` / `TEMPORAL_ACTIVITY_TASK_QUEUE` | `poc-http-ingress-b` |
| Worker | `node run-worker.js` (wraps `createCombinedWorker`), `POC_CAPTURE_TIMEOUT_MS` env (default 60000, set to 35000 for B4) |
| Sync bridge | `node sync-server.js`, listens on `POC_HTTP_PORT` (default `3940`) at `POST /poc/sync` |

All long-running processes were started via the `at now`/`setsid`-style
detach pattern (plain `nohup ... &` from the bash tool reliably hung the
tool call itself - see repo `AGENTS.md` Lessons Learned), with PIDs
captured to `/tmp/poc-b-*.pid` and killed by exact PID only.

## Experiments

### B1 — basic synchronous response — PASS

Flow: `n3` sets `statusCode: 201`, header `x-poc-node: n3`, JSON payload
echoing the request body.

```
$ curl -s -D - -X POST http://127.0.0.1:3940/poc/sync -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"hello":"world"}'
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
content-type: application/json
x-poc-node: n3
...
{"echoed":{"hello":"world"},"method":"POST","receivedAt":1789913973303}
```

Status 201, custom header, and JSON body all match the flow's descriptor. PASS.

### B2 — delayed response (~6s) — PASS

`n5`'s `delay` timeout set to `6` seconds; worker restarted to reload the flow file.

```
$ time curl -s -D - -X POST http://127.0.0.1:3940/poc/sync -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"n":"b2"}'
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
...
{"echoed":{"n":"b2"},"method":"POST","receivedAt":1789914147181}
real  0m6.385s
```

~6.4s wall time, matching the 6s delay plus overhead. PASS.

### B3 — ~30s delay — PASS

`n5`'s delay set to `30` seconds. Required bumping `BASE_ACTIVITY_OPTIONS.startToCloseTimeout`
from 30s to 40s (see diff above) - at exactly 30s the Activity's own
`StartToCloseTimeout` and the flow's own delay collide, aborting the
Activity with `NODE_TIMEOUT`/`Activity task timed out` before the delay
node itself could resolve normally.

```
$ time curl -s -D - -X POST http://127.0.0.1:3940/poc/sync -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"n":"b3"}' -m 45
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
...
{"echoed":{"n":"b3"},"method":"POST","receivedAt":1789914287467}
real  0m30.639s
```

~30.6s wall time. Nothing operationally awkward observed at this scale
with a plain `curl` (no default timeout unless one is passed) talking
directly to the bridge with no intervening proxy. Note for anyone putting
this behind a real reverse proxy: default `nginx proxy_read_timeout`
(60s) or many cloud load balancers' default idle timeouts (30-60s) would
need raising for delays anywhere near this range - not exercised here
since there is no proxy in this PoC's path. PASS.

### B4 — restart Activity worker while request open — PASS

Delay reduced to 15s for a feasible mid-flight kill window.
`POC_CAPTURE_TIMEOUT_MS=35000` (Capture's own pending timeout, well above
the 15s delay but below the 40s Activity `StartToCloseTimeout`).

```
$ curl ... -m 120 &      # started ~t=1789914469
$ kill <worker pid>      # killed at t=1789914477, ~8s into the request, mid-Activity (n5's delay in flight)
$ node run-worker.js &   # restarted immediately (new pid)
# curl finished after ~54s total (t=1789914527)
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
...
{"echoed":{"n":"b4"},"method":"POST","receivedAt":1789914526899}
```

sync-server log confirms one Workflow (`poc-http-ingress-b-1789914470012`)
started and later completed with the correct descriptor. The
in-progress `n5` Activity attempt was abandoned when its worker died;
Temporal's own `StartToCloseTimeout` (40s) eventually timed that attempt
out and a retry ran the delay node again on the restarted worker,
succeeding. Total end-to-end latency (~54s) reflects one full failed
attempt's timeout window plus one successful 15s retry - this is the
known, documented "at-least-once Activity" behavior from `AGENTS.md`
("Known limitations"), observed live: **not immediate resumption**, but
eventual, correct completion. The original HTTP client got the correct
response despite the mid-flight worker restart. PASS.

### B5 — kill the ingress process while request open — PASS

```
$ curl ... &                                  # started, workflow poc-http-ingress-b-1789914594983
$ kill <sync-server pid>                      # killed immediately after
# curl exited with empty output / non-zero (connection reset) - client-visible failure, as expected
$ temporal workflow describe --address 127.0.0.1:7249 --workflow-id poc-http-ingress-b-1789914594983
Results:
  RunTime         15.43s
  Status          COMPLETED
  Result          {"flowVersion":"...","lastMsg":{...,"payload":{"headers":{"x-poc-node":"n3"},"payload":{"echoed":{"n":"b5"},...},"statusCode":201}},"lastNode":"n4"}
```

The original curl connection died (empty response, connection reset) but
the Workflow itself kept running and COMPLETED independently with the
correct result, exactly as expected - proving the Workflow is durable
even though the HTTP socket (and the entire bridge process holding it)
is not. PASS.

### B6 — client disconnect — PASS

```
$ time timeout 2 curl -s -D - -X POST http://127.0.0.1:3940/poc/sync -d '{"n":"b6"}'
real   0m2.006s
exit: 124   # SIGTERM'd client-side after 2s
```

sync-server log (unbroken, no crash) shows the SAME workflow
(`poc-http-ingress-b-1789914631619`) started and, ~15s later (after the
delay node), completed with the full response descriptor logged. `grep -i
"error|exception"` on the sync-server log found nothing - `res.end()` on
the already-aborted connection completed silently rather than throwing;
the server remained fully responsive afterward (verified with a follow-up
`curl` that got a normal `201`). No uncaught exception, no crash, no
leak observed. PASS.

## Summary table

| Experiment | Result | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| B1 basic sync response | PASS | status/header/body match |
| B2 ~6s delay | PASS | `real 0m6.385s` |
| B3 ~30s delay | PASS | `real 0m30.639s`, required Activity timeout bump |
| B4 worker restart mid-flight | PASS | correct response after ~54s (1 failed attempt + 1 retry) |
| B5 ingress process killed mid-flight | PASS | `temporal workflow describe` shows `Status: COMPLETED` |
| B6 client disconnect | PASS | workflow completes, no uncaught exception, server stays healthy |

## Anything ugly / surprising

- The Capture pending-timeout (`capture.js` `DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS`, 5s) and
  the Activity's own `StartToCloseTimeout` (`workflows.js`
  `BASE_ACTIVITY_OPTIONS`, previously 30s) are two independent timers that
  must both comfortably exceed any `delay` node's duration, with the
  Capture timeout kept BELOW the Activity timeout (so a real Node-RED
  timeout surfaces as `NODE_TIMEOUT`, not a generic Activity-infra
  timeout). Neither is exposed as a normal CLI flag - `run-worker.js`
  bypasses the CLI to set Capture's timeout, and the Activity timeout
  required an actual (small, marked) code edit. This is a real gap for
  any flow with `delay`/long-running nodes - worth a dedicated
  configuration mechanism if this direction is pursued further.
- Killing the Activity worker mid-flight does NOT resume the in-progress
  Activity instantly - the abandoned attempt must first fully time out
  (up to its `StartToCloseTimeout`) before Temporal schedules a retry.
  For a 15s delay with a 40s Activity timeout, recovery took ~54s total,
  not ~15-20s as might be assumed. This is inherent to at-least-once
  Activity semantics without heartbeating, not a bug in this PoC.
- No proxy-timeout issues were observed at the ~30s scale tested (B3),
  since curl talked directly to the Node bridge - flagged above as a
  likely concern only once a real reverse proxy sits in front of this.
